indicators.note: a cover goes around whatever it protects, so one piece wraps around another
something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters leave their ordinary order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: An odd court hearing held over some university ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: TRIAL is rearranged to RITAL, and the U for university is slipped into its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A ritual is a set formal ceremony, often religious or traditional, performed the same way each time.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: newspaper slang for a huge, lurid headline
second meaning, taken literally: someone who shrieks in fear

explanation.surface: A lurid headline that plainly comes from a panicky person.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second meaning is a playful, literal reading: a scared person yells.
explanation.definitionFit: In journalism a screamer is a big sensational headline; literally it is anyone who shrieks, as a terrified person does.

clue.text: Fraud at Gloucestershire trials? One's brought to court

parts.note: the Badminton Horse Trials are held each year at Badminton House in Gloucestershire
a racket is a dishonest scheme or swindle

explanation.surface: A swindle uncovered at a famous horse-trials event in the English countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fraud at Gloucestershire trials' reads as a racket at Badminton, giving BADMINTON RACKET. Gloucestershire is an English county; its Badminton estate hosts a famous equestrian event and gave the sport its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A badminton racket is carried onto a court for play, so it is literally something brought to a court.

clue.text: Residence offering wine, two similar drinks added to menu, finally

parts.note: cha is a slang word for tea
the same drink under its usual name

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of the word is used

parts.note: the closing letter of menu

explanation.surface: A grand house serving wine, with a couple of matching drinks tacked onto the bill of fare.
explanation.walkthrough: The two similar drinks are both tea: CHA, the old British slang word, and TEA itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A French château is a country mansion, and many Bordeaux wine estates are called châteaux and name their wines after it.

clue.text: Young adult in gym is hotter, working out to keep slim

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one set of letters holds another inside
working out a problem means rearranging its parts until they fit, so these letters get reordered

parts.note: the eleven letters to be rearranged
slim and thin are synonyms

explanation.surface: A young adult at the gym, sweating hard and exercising to stay slim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working out' fits the gym picture so well that it hides its role as the rearranging signal; THIN goes in just before the final G.
explanation.definitionFit: A thirty-something is a person aged between thirty and forty, a stage still counted as early adulthood.

clue.text: Craft of war ludicrous, a painter has claimed

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: having claimed something is holding it as yours, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician, a painter
ludicrous and mad both mean absurd

explanation.surface: A painter has taken up a ridiculous wartime vessel as their subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' is plural here: a fleet of warships, not a skill. RA, a Royal Academician, is the usual crossword painter.
explanation.definitionFit: An armada is a large fleet of warships, so it is a collection of war vessels.

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only a part of the following words is used

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A rather fiendish, anguished singing voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tortured' looks like an invitation to rearrange letters, but it simply contributes its first two letters to the run.
explanation.definitionFit: An alto is a low female or high male singing range, one of the standard choir parts.

indicators.note: to finish off is to take away the end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: disco was the dance music craze of the 1970s

explanation.surface: An instruction to wrap up some seventies dance music for a recording.
explanation.walkthrough: DISCO loses its final O.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc is a gramophone record or other recording, as in a hit disc or a disc jockey.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a common deciduous tree
second meaning: the powdery residue left by burning

explanation.surface: A tree is all that is left standing after a blaze.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about a burnt forest, but it splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a familiar woodland tree and also the grey powder left once something has burnt.

clue.text: Lolita originally penned by English author? I don't think so!

indicators.note: something penned is enclosed as in a pen, so one piece is shut inside another

parts.note: Thomas Hardy, the English novelist

indicators.note: originally refers to how something began, so the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of Lolita

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea that Lolita was written by an English novelist, since Nabokov was Russian-American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penned' looks like writing a book, but it means enclosed: the L goes inside HARDY.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardly expresses strong doubt or denial, an informal retort meaning scarcely or certainly not.

clue.text: Something to keep locks in use where artefacts kept

indicators.note: to lock someone in is to shut them inside a room, so one thing ends up enclosed

parts.note: people are told to keep mum, meaning stay silent
taken as written

explanation.surface: A device for holding hair in place, still in use where old objects are displayed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' suggests hair, but it is a verb meaning shuts in. The phrase 'keep mum' means say nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A museum is a building where historical, artistic or scientific objects are stored and exhibited to the public.

indicators.note: after means following, so this part is placed behind the other

parts.note: jack and tar are both old slang for a sailor

indicators.note: playing an instrument rearranges sounds, and here the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A man called Herb takes his turn at the organ after Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' looks like a man's name in the surface but is the definition. Jack and tar are both crossword sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarragon is an aromatic culinary plant with narrow leaves, used in French cooking and béarnaise sauce.

clue.text: A tangle centrally, a main internal passage

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to tangle threads is to twist them into a muddle, so these letters are knotted into a new sequence

parts.note: fourteen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A knot sits right in the middle of a building's principal corridor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centrally' looks like an instruction to take middle letters, but it is just part of the mix, and 'tangle' is the verb doing the mixing.
explanation.definitionFit: The digestive tract is the continuous tube food travels through, from mouth to anus, a passage inside the body.

parts.note: taken as written
UK, the United Kingdom, stands for British

explanation.surface: Simply a bird found in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a plain description, but 'British' supplies UK after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Auks are diving seabirds of northern waters, a family including puffins, guillemots and razorbills.

indicators.note: behind means coming after, so this part is placed second

parts.note: a spar is a beam or pole, like a rafter
a row is a line, like a queue

explanation.surface: A bird waits in line behind someone up in the roof beams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is only a link: the bird is found in the wordplay that follows, read in the order 'rafter' then 'queue'.
explanation.definitionFit: The sparrow is a small brown songbird, very common in towns and gardens.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a professional, someone who earns money for their work

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as 'someone has been paid for', but the split comes before the last word: one who is paid, and in favour.
explanation.definitionFit: A professional is someone who earns a living at an activity, and the Latin preposition meaning in favour of is used in English too.

indicators.note: something subversive overturns the established order, so these letters are thrown out of theirs

parts.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A rebel agrees, throwing their worries out of the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subversive' sounds like a description of a person, but it signals the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: To forsake is to abandon or renounce, which is what casting something aside means as a verb.

parts.note: as in 'ready, steady, go' or 'all set'
taken as written
a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: A reserve player on a squad, prepared and waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' looks like a noun for a substitute player, but it is the verb: to keep something back.
explanation.definitionFit: To set aside money or time is to keep it back for later, the same as to reserve it.

parts.note: of can mean concerning, as in 'tales of the sea'
a fence is a barrier

explanation.surface: A complaint about a boundary in the wrong place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' usually signals wrapping or turning, but here it is simply OF, meaning concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: An offence is a crime or misdeed, so as a noun it is a wrong done to someone.

clue.text: Title to order, cost left out

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or awry, as a dislocated joint is out, signalling a jumble

parts.note: all fifteen letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction for buying a title, with the price omitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To order' and 'left out' both look like instructions, but every letter from 'to' to 'left' goes into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor of Letters is an academic honour, a higher degree in the humanities, carried before a name like Dr.

indicators.note: erasing the head of something wipes out its first part, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: a sticker is an adhesive label

explanation.surface: Someone has removed the word 'head' from a label and put 'heart' instead.
explanation.walkthrough: STICKER loses its first letter. Ticker is informal for the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Ticker is slang for the heart, from the regular beating that sounds like a clock.

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a tangy pickle or sauce served with food

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys their sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like enjoying a sauce, but the verb and the noun are two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb meaning to enjoy keenly and a noun for a chopped pickle served alongside meals.

clue.text: Frosty, relative has admitted — it's difficult to get on!

indicators.note: admitting someone lets them in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: an uncle is a relative
frosty and icy both mean very cold

explanation.surface: A frosty relative has confessed that they are hard to get along with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on' means get along with in the surface, but literally means mount: a one-wheeled cycle is hard to climb onto.
explanation.definitionFit: A unicycle has a single wheel and no support, so climbing aboard and balancing is notoriously tricky.

clue.text: Usual thing, choice of extremes in naturism?

indicators.note: the extremes of anything are its two ends, so the outermost letters are used

parts.note: the opening letter of naturism
or offers a choice between two things
the closing letter of naturism

explanation.surface: Is going naked the ordinary thing, or an extreme option?
explanation.walkthrough: The 'choice of extremes' is N or M, the first and last letters of naturism, read literally as N OR M.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is the standard or typical pattern, the thing that is customary or expected.

indicators.note: performing a piece turns it into something new, so the letters get reworked

parts.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A detective takes to the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Performs' looks like the detective's action, but it signals rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hustle was a popular disco line dance of the 1970s, named after the hit song.

explanation.surface: A light wind making for an easy trip on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: The sailing picture links the two, but the second meaning is figurative: an easy task.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a gentle wind, and informally a task so easy it needs no effort at all.

indicators.note: first refers to the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of cellists
a play or player that is currently performing is on

explanation.surface: The lead cellist picks up a violin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' wants to be a violin to match the cellists, but it means a swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiddle is British slang for a swindle or scam, and a con is the same kind of dishonest trick.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a shallow container for food
second meaning: a very attractive person

explanation.surface: Someone who breaks crockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smasher' suggests breaking plates, but it is British slang for a gorgeous person, also called a dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish is a serving vessel like a plate, and informally a good-looking person, as a smasher is.
